title: Beef Bourguignon
subtitle: French beef braised in red wine with lardons and mushrooms
excerpt: The supreme French beef braise: chuck or shin braised for hours in a full bottle of red wine with lardons, mushrooms, and pearl onions until the beef is tender enough to cut with a spoon and the sauce is glossy and deeply savoury.

recipe.sourceNotes: Beef Bourguignon (boeuf bourguignon) is the defining beef stew of French bourgeois cooking and one of the most celebrated dishes to emerge from the Burgundy region, which produces both its two principal ingredients: the Charolais beef and the wine. The dish was popularised internationally by Julia Child's 1961 Mastering the Art of French Cooking, which gave the dish step-by-step instructions in English for the first time and made it a centrepiece of mid-century American dinner party cooking. The canonical preparation marinates the beef overnight in the wine (though many modern recipes skip this step), then braises it long and slow. The garnish of lardons, pearl onions, and mushrooms that surrounds the finished braise is prepared separately so each element retains its distinct texture and character. The sauce is typically thickened by reducing alone or with a small amount of flour; cornflour is not used.

content.text: Brown the beef in dry batches over high heat; any moisture on the surface will create steam and prevent the Maillard reaction. A good dark crust on each piece of beef is essential to the flavour of the finished sauce. The braise should barely tremble throughout cooking: never boil. If the sauce is too thin at the end, remove the beef and reduce the sauce over high heat before returning the beef.

items.preparation: cut into 5 cm chunks; patted dry
full bottle; a good Burgundy or Pinot Noir
small shallots or pearl onions, peeled and left whole
peeled and cut into 3 cm pieces

content.text: Heat the oil in a large casserole over high heat. Season the beef. Brown in batches until deeply coloured on all sides. Do not crowd the pan. Remove. Fry the lardons until golden. Remove. Brown the shallots in the butter until golden all over. Remove. Reduce to medium heat. Fry the carrot and garlic for 3 minutes. Add the flour and tomato purée and stir for 1 minute.

Pour in the wine and stock, scraping the bottom of the pot. Return the beef and lardons. Add the thyme, bay leaves, salt, and pepper. The liquid should just cover the beef. Bring to a very gentle simmer, cover, and cook over the lowest heat (or in a 150 C oven) for 2 hours 30 minutes to 3 hours until the beef is completely tender.

When the beef is almost done, fry the mushrooms in a little butter over high heat until golden. Add the browned shallots back to the casserole for the final 30 minutes of braising. Remove the bay leaves. Taste and adjust the seasoning. Stir in the mushrooms. Serve with mashed potato or crusty bread.
